Barnes & Noble’s Book of the Year is…
Barnes and Noble announced its 2026 Book of the Year, as well as its Books of the Year in Nonfiction, Children’s, and Children’s Gifts. The winners are:
Whale Harbor by Mary Beth Keane (2026 B&N Book of the Year): A family saga about brotherhood and immigration from Ireland to Montana from the author of Ask Again, Yes

This Vast Enterprise: A New History of Lewis & Clark by Craig Fehrman (2026 B&N Nonfiction Book of the Year): An in-depth account of the Lewis and Clark expedition featuring new perspectives and recently discovered materials

The Unlikely Tale of Chase and Finnegan (B&N Exclusive Edition) by Jasmine Warga (2026 B&N Children’s Book of the Year): A heartwarming story about two unlikely friends from the author of Other Words for Home

Is This a Plum? A Peek-Through Picture Book by Dan Ojari and Finn Ojari (2026 B&N Children’s Gift Book of the Year): An interactive picture book from a father-son duo that teaches the littles about perspective
Barnes and Noble’s Books of the Year are described as the titles their booksellers are raving about. Previous winners include:
Mona’s Eyes (2025 B&N Book of the Year) by Thomas Schlesser
James (2024 B&N Book of the Year, Pulitzer Prize Winner, and National Book Award Winner) by Percival Everett
The Heaven & Earth Grocery Store: A Novel (B&N Exclusive Edition) by James McBride

It’s largely comprised of buzzy and bestselling books, but there are also a few less-talked-about books, and the book that nabbed the #1 spot may surprise you.
Here are the titles that round out the top 10:
American Hagwon by Min Jin Lee
Exit Party by Emily St. John Mandel
The Vanishing Family: Love, Fate, and the Quest to End Dementia by Robert Kolker

We need vocal advocates for free speech

When you think of book bans in the 2020s, one of the books that immediately comes to mind is Gender Queer. Maia Kobabe’s memoir was published in the spring of 2019 to tremendous praise and acclaim. It earne an Alex Award, presented annually to books published for adult readers but with particular appeal to teen readers.

During this fall’s Banned Books Week, the American Library Association’s Office of Intellectual Freedom (OIF) released a list of the 150 most banned books in America since the OIF launched in 1967. Gender Queer tops the list.

Perhaps what’s most remarkable during the nonstop, virulent attacks on Gender Queer—which by virtue of the comic being a memoir, are direct attacks on Kobabe eirself—is that Kobabe has not backed down.
E has been a relentless advocate for other authors feeling the sting of book bans, pouring incredible time, energy, and effort into championing the work of other comics.

When Kobabe learned that Gender Queer was the most banned book during the life of the OIF, it’s no surprise e was highlighting a project that furthered the realities of contemporary literary censorship. Kobabe served as curator and editor for a potent project from Xtra Magazine, sharing a moving and insightful series of comics about the realities of book bans.

In this exclusive interview, Kobabe talks about eir experiences with censorship and where that’s helped eir commit to continuing to speak up and out, as well as amplify the array of queer comics publishing both online and in print.

“The challenges against Gender Queer really helped clarify the purpose of my work,” Kobabe explains. “I want to write books and tell stories which make it easier, safer, and more joyful for trans and nonbinary people to exist in this world.”

New Indigenous books to read this month

Deb Haaland made history this month when she became the first Indigenous American woman to be elected governor, just as Native American Heritage Month began. This first is a cause for celebration, and it’s also a shame that it took this long.
This is why heritage months exist in the first place. This country is still catching up to where it should be, and it’s important to learn about the history and experiences of our community members.
The books below allow us to do just that.
A Voice Like Mine by Deb Haaland – Governor-elect Haaland’s memoir chronicling a lifetime of firsts as a trailblazing cabinet secretary, organizer, and congresswoman.

Children of Owl by Darcie Little Badger and Abigail Rajunov – YA fantasy from a Newbery Honor winner about three cousins and the creatures—real and other-worldly, good and evil—that surround their trailer park.

Off the Reservation by Stephen Graham Jones – A thrilling sequel from one of our most exciting living horror writers, where a group of activists sets out to return the bones of a Blackfeet boy taken to an infamous residential school.
Sunflower Season by Danica Nava – A burnt-out city girl heads to rural Oklahoma to try her hand at running a sunflower farm in this sweet second-chance romance.

I don’t know about you, but historical fiction has often been a better history teacher than straight-up school. Furthermore, some of the best historical fiction I’ve read takes often-explored moments and shows a whole new side to them.
Such is the case with these books that take place during the Renaissance.

The Last Prince of Florence by Zoe Sivak: The Medici family is a popular subject, but I haven’t seen much on Alessandro de’ Medici, the first Black person to be the head of state in the modern Western world. Here, Sivak explores how his mother, a brown-skinned girl who arrived in Santo Spirito with a dagger strapped to her chest, plots to put her son on the throne.

Graceless Heart by Isabel Ibañez: In this adult romantasy, sculptress Ravenna reveals her talent for magic in order to save her brother. Thing is, magic is forbidden, and she’s soon kidnapped by a powerful family, and made to complete a task that, if failed, will mean her death. War is brewing, alliances are made, and Ravenna has to navigate it all.

The Familiar by Leigh Bardugo: Here’s another romantasy—albeit a more macabre one—in which the protagonist reveals her magic to disastrous results. For scullery maid Luzia, her cruel mistress finding out about her ability is beneficial at first, until it turns into her being used as a political pawn. Then there is the issue of the immortal familiar whose help she needs—and the Spanish Inquisition that rages on in the background. —EE
Did you know? Stevenson created the story for what would become Treasure Island to amuse his stepson during a fit of bad weather that kept the family indoors.
